name: Lopaka
tagline: Browser based layout editor for small embedded displays that spits out C++ draw code for U8g2, Adafruit GFX, LVGL and friends.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The idea is simple enough that an agent will happily build it: a canvas locked to 128x64, draggable rects, lines, text and imported bitmaps, then a code generator that emits draw calls. That gets you most of the way for one target library in one sitting. The part that eats a weekend and then some is pixel fidelity: matching the exact glyph bitmaps and baseline metrics of dozens of bundled fonts across U8g2, Adafruit GFX and LVGL, so the preview is actually what the panel shows. If you only ever target one library and two fonts, roll your own and never think about it again. If you hop between Flipper Zero, ESP-IDF and TFT_eSPI, you are rebuilding a font pipeline, not an editor.
coreLoopDIY: A local canvas editor sized to your display where you place shapes, text and dithered bitmaps, then copy out generated U8g2 C++ draw calls.
requirements: A real display to verify the preview is not lying
Willingness to hand-pick which font bitmaps you bundle
whatYouLose: Export targets beyond the one you implement: U8g2, Adafruit GFX, LVGL, TFT_eSPI, ESP-IDF, Flipper Zero all have different idioms
The big bundled font catalog with correct widths, baselines and kerning per library
Image import that already knows about thresholds, dithering and inverted panels
Multi screen project management and saved layouts you can come back to
Someone else tracking upstream library API changes for you
moatNotes: The moat is not the editor, it is the accumulated font and library mapping tables that make the preview match the hardware.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the alternative to Lopaka is not a weekend project, it is flashing the board, squinting at a 0.96 inch OLED, nudging a Y coordinate by two pixels and flashing again. Paying removes an entire feedback loop measured in minutes per iteration, and it does it for whatever library the current project happens to use. That is worth more than a self-hosted editor that is accurate for exactly one font on exactly one driver.
notes: Fine thing to clone if you live on one display and one library forever. The grind is font fidelity, not drag and drop.
prompt:
Build a local, offline web app called "tinylayout": a pixel editor for monochrome embedded displays that exports C++ draw code.

Stack, no substitutions: Vite + React + TypeScript, Zustand for state, plain HTML canvas for rendering, no backend, no accounts, no telemetry, no network calls at runtime. State persists to localStorage only.

Target: monochrome 1-bit displays. Canvas size is configurable with presets 128x64, 128x32, 256x64, and custom width/height. Render at integer zoom (1x to 8x) with a visible pixel grid above 3x.

In scope:
- Layer list with add, delete, reorder, rename, lock, hide, and arrow-key nudging of the selected layer by 1px (10px with shift).
- Layer types: pixel, line, rect (outline/filled), circle (outline/filled), text, bitmap.
- Text layers use bundled bitmap fonts only. Embed two public domain fixed-size fonts as TypeScript glyph data: a 5x7 and an 8x8. Draw glyphs pixel by pixel from that data so the preview is byte-for-byte what the device will show.
- Bitmap layers: drag a PNG or JPG in, scale it, convert to 1-bit with a selectable threshold slider and a Floyd-Steinberg dithering toggle, with an invert option.
- Right panel shows numeric X, Y, W, H and type-specific props for the selected layer.
- Export panel with two tabs: "U8g2" and "XBM". U8g2 emits a function body of u8g2.drawLine/drawBox/drawFrame/drawDisc/drawCircle/drawXBMP calls in placement order. Text layers and bitmap layers both export as XBM byte arrays plus a drawXBMP call, so nothing depends on device-side font availability. XBM tab emits the whole flattened screen as one 1-bit array.
- A "copy to clipboard" button on each export tab, and JSON project import/export to a file.

Out of scope, do not build: LVGL or TFT_eSPI or Flipper Zero exporters, color displays, animation, cloud sync, user accounts, a font importer, undo history beyond a simple 20-step undo/redo stack.

Correctness requirements: the generated code must compile under Arduino with U8g2 as-is; the preview must be rendered from the same rasterizer used to produce the XBM bytes, so there is exactly one code path for pixels. Write a small unit test with Vitest that rasterizes a known layout and asserts the exported byte array.

Finish with a README: how to run dev, how to build static files, where the font data lives, and a one-paragraph note that only U8g2 output is supported.
